description: Errors found while handling #include / #define lines, before real compilation starts.

rules.title: Header file not found
rules.what: The compiler cannot find the header file `{header}` that you asked for with `#include`.
why: The header name is misspelled (for example `stdoi.h` instead of `stdio.h`).
It is an old Turbo C header that modern compilers do not have (`conio.h`, `iostream.h`, `graphics.h`).
It is your own header file but it is not in the same folder as your program.
fix: Check the spelling of the header name on line {line}.
rules.tip: A *fatal* error stops the compiler immediately, so nothing after this line was checked yet. Fix it and compile again.
samples: stdoi.h: No such file or directory
iostream.h: No such file or directory

rules.title: Unknown # directive
rules.what: `#{directive}` is not a preprocessor command. A line that starts with `#` must use a known directive such as `#include` or `#define`.
why: A typing mistake in the directive name (`#inlcude`, `#defien`, `#incldue`).
rules.tip: Because the #include line was ignored, functions such as printf may now also look 'undeclared'. Those messages disappear once this line is fixed.
samples: invalid preprocessing directive #inlcude; did you mean #include?

rules.title: Extra text after #include / #define line
rules.what: There is something extra at the end of your `#{directive}` line - usually a semicolon.
why: Preprocessor lines are not C statements, so they never end with `;`.
fix: Delete the `;` (or other extra text) at the end of line {line}.
samples: extra tokens at end of #include directive

rules.title: Badly written #include
rules.what: The `#include` line is not written correctly. The header name must be inside `< >` (standard headers) or `" "` (your own files).
why: Quotes or brackets mixed up, e.g. `#include <stdio.h"`.
fix: Write it exactly like `#include <stdio.h>` (or `#include "myheader.h"` for your own file).

rules.title: Semicolon at the end of a #define
rules.what: The macro `{macro}` is defined with a semicolon at the end (`#define {macro} {value}`). The preprocessor pastes that `;` everywhere you use `{macro}`, which breaks the code on line {line}.
why: `#define` is a text replacement, not a statement. Everything after the name - including `;` - is copied into your code.
fix: Remove the `;` at the end of the `#define` line (line {macro_line}).

example.wrong:
#define SIZE 10;
int a[SIZE];   /* becomes int a[10;]; */

rules.title: Macro defined twice
rules.what: The macro `{macro}` is defined with `#define` more than once, with different values.
why: Two `#define {macro}` lines, or a header that already defines the same name.
fix: Keep only one `#define {macro}`, or give the second one a different name.

rules.title: Unbalanced #if / #endif
rules.what: The `#if` / `#ifdef` / `#ifndef` lines and their `#endif` lines do not pair up.
why: An `#endif` is missing, or there is one `#endif` too many.
fix: Every `#if`, `#ifdef` or `#ifndef` needs exactly one matching `#endif`.
